Ethical review, clear hypotheses and behavior-based outcome measures make experiments credible and safe in sensitive settings.

sections.heading: What A/B testing is and why it matters
paragraphs: A/B testing is a controlled experiment. Two or more versions of something, such as a message, a form, a process or an offer, are presented to comparable groups of people, usually through random assignment, and the resulting behavior is compared. Because the groups are otherwise similar, differences in outcome can be attributed to the difference in version with reasonable confidence. This is the same logic that underpins clinical trials, applied to everyday business decisions.

Technology companies adopted A/B testing early because digital products make it easy to show different versions to different users and to measure what happens. The underlying principle is not specific to software, however. Any organization that makes decisions about how to communicate, sell, serve or support people is making implicit predictions about behavior. A/B testing makes those predictions explicit and checks them. Without testing, organizations tend to adopt whatever the most senior or persuasive person prefers, which is not the same as what works.

sections.heading: What can be tested outside the tech industry
paragraphs: The range of testable decisions is much wider than most organizations assume. Communications are the most obvious example: letters, emails, text reminders, brochures and call scripts can all be varied and compared. Processes can be tested too, such as the order of steps in an application, the timing of a follow-up call or the default option in an enrollment form. Service designs, including how appointments are scheduled or how a sales conversation is structured, are also candidates.

In healthcare, organizations can test reminder timing, the framing of health information or the design of a patient onboarding sequence. In financial services and lending, they can test disclosure formats, application flows or outreach scripts. Associations and nonprofits can test membership renewal messages or donor appeals. Inside organizations, leaders can test variations in training formats, meeting structures or internal communications. In each case, the principle is the same: compare alternatives and measure behavior.
bullets: Reminder timing and channel for appointments, payments or renewals.
Framing and format of letters, disclosures and educational materials.
Order of steps and defaults in applications and enrollment forms.
Call scripts and conversation structures in sales and service.
Onboarding sequences for patients, members, customers or new employees.
Training formats and internal communication approaches.

sections.heading: Adapting experiments to real-world constraints
paragraphs: Organizations outside the technology sector often face constraints that make classic A/B testing harder. Volumes may be too low to detect small differences quickly. Randomizing individuals may be impractical when people interact with the same staff or share information with each other. Regulations, union agreements or professional norms may limit what can be varied. These constraints are real, but they rarely make experimentation impossible. They call for design choices rather than abandonment.

Several alternatives are available. Cluster randomization assigns whole locations, teams or time periods to different versions. Staggered rollouts introduce a change in some sites before others, creating a natural comparison. Structured pilots with carefully chosen comparison groups provide weaker but still useful evidence. Longer test periods can compensate for low volume. The key is to decide on the design, measures and decision rule before the test begins, so that results are interpreted honestly.

sections.heading: Ethics and trust in experimentation
paragraphs: Experimenting with how people are treated raises legitimate ethical questions, especially in healthcare, education, finance and public services. The guiding principle is that every version tested should be acceptable on its own terms. Testing two reasonable reminder messages is very different from withholding a beneficial service from one group. Where an intervention is clearly better, it should simply be offered. Experiments are for genuine uncertainty about which reasonable option works best.

Good practice includes review by an appropriate body, such as an institutional review board in research settings or an internal ethics or compliance group elsewhere. Consent and transparency should match the setting and the risk. Data should be handled with care and minimized where possible. Organizations should also consider fairness, checking whether a version helps some groups while disadvantaging others. Done this way, A/B testing strengthens trust, because decisions rest on evidence rather than on preference or assumption.
bullets: Test only options that are acceptable on their own.
Seek appropriate ethics or compliance review.
Match transparency and consent to the level of risk.
Check effects across groups for fairness.

sections.heading: Designing a good test
paragraphs: A good A/B test starts with a hypothesis, not a hunch. The hypothesis should name a behavior, a population and a predicted change, and it should be grounded in research about why the current behavior occurs. The outcome measure should be behavioral and meaningful, such as completed applications, kept appointments or renewed memberships, rather than opens or clicks alone. The test should vary one thing at a time where possible, so the result can be interpreted clearly.

Sample size and duration should be estimated in advance, and the decision rule should be written down: what result will lead to adopting the new version, keeping the old one or testing further. Results should be examined by segment, because an average effect can hide very different responses among different behavioral types. Finally, every result should be documented, including null and negative results. A library of tested hypotheses becomes an organizational asset that prevents teams from repeating experiments or relearning old lessons.

sections.heading: How Datalidy applies A/B testing beyond tech
paragraphs: Experimentation is the Test phase of Datalidy's Observe, Signal, Design, Test, Scale method, and it is where the firm's Behavioral Signals Design methodology proves its value. Predictive KPIs defined in the Signal phase become outcome measures, and interventions created in the Design phase become the versions under test. Datalidy designs A/B tests where volume allows and structured pilots where it does not, drawing on research methods and clinical research practice to keep tests rigorous and ethical.

The firm has supported experimentation for organizations in healthcare and digital health, automotive, mortgage lending, financial services, associations and education. It also helps teams build internal capability, so that testing becomes routine rather than a special project. That includes training staff to write hypotheses, choose behavioral outcome measures and interpret results without overreading them. In the Scale phase, Datalidy helps embed successful interventions and the habits of experimentation through dashboards, process design and leadership coaching, so learning continues after an engagement ends.

faqs.q: How many people do we need for an A/B test?
faqs.a: It depends on how large a difference you expect and how variable the outcome is. Detecting small effects requires larger groups, while large effects can be seen with fewer people. A sample size estimate before the test prevents ending it too early or running it longer than necessary. When volume is limited, longer test periods, cluster designs or structured pilots can still produce useful evidence.

faqs.q: Is A/B testing appropriate in healthcare?
faqs.a: Yes, when designed responsibly. Many health organizations test reminder messages, educational materials, scheduling processes and patient onboarding. The key conditions are that every version tested is acceptable care or communication, that appropriate ethics or compliance review is in place, and that data is protected. Experiments should address genuine uncertainty, never withhold something known to be beneficial.

faqs.q: What if a test shows no difference?
faqs.a: A null result is still information. It may mean the change did not affect behavior, that the test lacked enough volume to detect a modest effect, or that different groups responded in opposite ways. Examine results by segment, check whether the intervention was delivered as intended, and document the finding. Knowing what does not work prevents wasted investment and sharpens the next hypothesis.

insights.title: Finding the Conversion Points in a Customer Journey
insights.meta_title: How to Find Conversion Points in a Customer Journey
insights.meta_description: Conversion points are the moments where a customer journey is decided. Learn how to find them in your data, validate them, and design interventions around them.
insights.summary: How to identify the few behavioral moments in a customer journey where outcomes are actually decided, and how to measure and improve them with evidence.
insights.dek: Customer journeys contain many steps, but only a few decide the outcome. Finding those conversion points tells an organization where to focus design, measurement and experimentation for the greatest effect.
key_takeaways: Conversion points are behavioral moments where the paths of people who reach an outcome and those who do not begin to diverge.
They are often different from the stages an organization already tracks, such as funnel steps defined by its own systems.
Finding them requires connecting data across systems and combining sequence analysis with qualitative research.
Each validated conversion point should anchor a predictive KPI and a set of tested interventions.

sections.heading: What a conversion point is
paragraphs: A conversion point is a behavioral moment in a journey where the eventual outcome is effectively decided. Before it, people who will convert and people who will not look broadly similar. After it, their paths diverge. The term comes from marketing, where conversion usually means a purchase or sign-up, but the idea applies to any outcome that depends on behavior: a patient beginning a treatment plan, a member renewing, an employee adopting a new system or a prospect moving from interest to commitment.

Conversion points are not the same as funnel stages. Funnel stages are usually defined by an organization's own systems: visited, registered, quoted, purchased. Conversion points are defined by behavior and its relationship to the outcome. A conversion point might fall inside a stage, such as whether a prospect returns to a configuration tool a second time, or between stages, such as how quickly a new customer receives a first response. Identifying these moments is what makes a customer journey map useful for decisions rather than only for description.

sections.heading: Why most organizations miss them
paragraphs: Most organizations measure what their systems record, and their systems record transactions and stage changes rather than behavior in context. A CRM shows that a lead became an opportunity, but not the sequence of interactions that made it happen. A web analytics platform shows visits and clicks, but not the call that followed. A patient record shows a missed appointment, but not the reminder that never arrived. The data needed to see conversion points is usually spread across systems that were never integrated.

Assumptions also get in the way. Teams often believe they already know where the journey breaks, typically at price, at the application form or at the final decision. Sometimes they are right. Often the decisive moment occurs much earlier and is far less visible, such as an unclear first interaction, a delay that signals indifference, or a small confusion that erodes confidence. Without evidence, attention and investment go to the assumed moment rather than the real one.
bullets: Systems record stage changes, not the behaviors that cause them.
Data for a single journey is often split across several platforms.
Teams focus on the final decision rather than the early moments that shape it.
Untested beliefs about where people drop out direct investment to the wrong place.

sections.heading: How to find conversion points in the data
paragraphs: Finding conversion points starts with the outcome. Define it precisely, then assemble the behavioral history of people who reached it and people who did not, across every system that records part of the journey. Linking these records is often the hardest step, and it may require careful matching and attention to privacy and governance. Once connected, the data can be examined as sequences of behavior over time rather than as isolated counts.

Several analytical approaches help. Comparing the paths of converters and non-converters shows where they begin to diverge. Survival and time-to-event analysis reveals moments when drop-off accelerates. Sequence analysis identifies common patterns and the points where they branch. Predictive models can rank which early behaviors best predict the outcome. None of these methods is definitive alone. Together, and interpreted with domain knowledge, they produce a short list of candidate conversion points worth investigating further.
bullets: Define the outcome and the population precisely.
Connect behavioral records across systems at the individual level.
Compare the paths of people who did and did not reach the outcome.
Look for moments where paths diverge or drop-off accelerates.
Shortlist candidate conversion points for qualitative investigation.

sections.heading: Validate with qualitative research and experiments
paragraphs: Data can point to where paths diverge, but it cannot always explain why. A behavior that predicts conversion may be a cause, a symptom of an underlying difference, or a coincidence. Qualitative research helps distinguish among these. Interviews, contextual inquiry and usability testing at the candidate moment often reveal what people are thinking, what they expected and what made them hesitate. Those insights turn a statistical pattern into an understanding of behavior that can guide design.

Experiments provide the strongest validation. If a candidate conversion point is genuinely causal, then an intervention that improves behavior at that moment should improve the outcome. A/B tests or structured pilots that change the experience at that point and measure downstream results test this directly. Conversion points that survive both qualitative scrutiny and experimental testing deserve a permanent place in measurement and management. Those that do not should be set aside, however intuitive they seemed.

sections.heading: Designing around conversion points
paragraphs: Once validated, conversion points become the organizing principle for improvement. Each one should have a predictive KPI that measures behavior at that moment, an owner responsible for it, and a set of interventions under test. Interventions may involve simplifying a step, adding a well-timed prompt, clarifying information, changing a default, improving service response or rethinking messaging. The Fogg Behavior Model is a useful lens: at each conversion point, ask whether motivation, ability or a prompt is the missing element.

Conversion points also interact with behavioral segments. Different groups of people may struggle at different moments or for different reasons. A careful comparer may stall at a moment where information is unclear, while a fast decider may stall where a process is slow. Designing interventions by segment at each conversion point produces more precise and effective changes than treating every customer the same way at every step. It also makes results easier to interpret, because each test targets a specific group at a specific moment.

sections.heading: How Datalidy finds and improves conversion points
paragraphs: Identifying conversion points is a central step in Datalidy's Behavioral Signals Design methodology. The firm starts from the outcome, maps the full journey and the data around it, often across systems that were never integrated, and identifies the few behavioral moments that actually drive results, along with the behavioral types that move through them differently. In the Observe phase, journey mapping, interviews and user testing ground the analysis in real experience.

In the Signal phase, behavioral data analysis confirms which moments matter and defines predictive KPIs around them. The Design and Test phases then develop and validate interventions through A/B tests and pilots. Datalidy has applied this approach to purchase and ownership journeys for an automotive brand, sales processes in lending, member journeys in associations and patient journeys in digital health. In each case, the aim is to focus effort where behavior, and therefore the outcome, is really decided.

faqs.q: How many conversion points does a typical journey have?
faqs.a: Usually only a few that truly matter, even in long and complex journeys. Many steps influence the outcome a little, while a small number influence it a great deal. The goal of analysis is to find those few, so attention and investment can concentrate where they have the most effect. A list of many conversion points usually means the analysis has not yet separated signal from noise.

faqs.q: Are conversion points only relevant to sales and marketing?
faqs.a: No. Any outcome that depends on a sequence of behavior has conversion points. In healthcare they might be the first refill or the second appointment. In technology adoption they might be the first time a user completes a real task in a new system. In employee onboarding they might be the first meaningful contribution. The method is the same regardless of setting.

faqs.q: What if we cannot connect data across our systems?
faqs.a: Start with what is available and supplement it with qualitative research. Interviews, observation and journey mapping can identify likely conversion points even without integrated data, and targeted data collection can then test them. Partial integration focused on a specific outcome is often far easier than a full data platform project, and it can deliver useful insight while longer-term integration work continues.

insights.title: The Psychology of Technology Adoption
insights.meta_title: The Psychology of Technology Adoption, Explained
insights.meta_description: Why people adopt or resist new technology: perceived usefulness, ease of use, social influence and habit, plus how to design rollouts that lead to lasting use.
insights.summary: The psychological forces that determine whether people adopt or resist new technology, and how leaders can design rollouts that turn installation into lasting, meaningful use.
insights.dek: Buying or launching technology is easy compared with getting people to use it well. Technology adoption is a behavioral challenge, shaped by perceived usefulness, ease of use, social influence, habit and trust.
key_takeaways: Technology adoption is a sequence of behaviors, from first trial to sustained, meaningful use, rather than a single decision.
Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, central to Davis' Technology Acceptance Model, strongly shape willingness to adopt.
Social influence, as described in Rogers' diffusion of innovations, determines how new practices spread through groups and organizations.
Measuring early usage behaviors gives leaders predictive signals of adoption long before final results are visible.

sections.heading: Why technology adoption is a behavioral problem
paragraphs: Organizations invest heavily in new technology, from customer platforms and clinical systems to analytics tools and AI assistants. Yet installation is not adoption. Many systems are technically live while people continue to rely on old workarounds, use only a small portion of available features, or abandon the tool after initial curiosity fades. Customers face the same pattern with new products and services. The gap between availability and use is where much of the expected value of technology is lost.

Technology adoption is fundamentally about behavior. People must notice the technology, decide to try it, succeed in using it, integrate it into their routines and continue using it when the novelty is gone. Each step is influenced by perception, ability, social context and habit. Treating adoption as a training or communication problem alone tends to address only part of this sequence. Treating it as a behavioral design problem addresses the whole of it.

sections.heading: Usefulness and ease of use
paragraphs: Fred Davis' Technology Acceptance Model identified two beliefs that strongly shape whether people intend to use a technology: perceived usefulness, the belief that it will help them do their job or reach their goals, and perceived ease of use, the belief that using it will be free of unnecessary effort. These are perceptions, not objective qualities. A powerful system that people believe is hard to use, or irrelevant to their real work, will struggle regardless of its technical merits.

This has practical implications. Usefulness must be demonstrated in terms of the user's own priorities, not the organization's. A clinician cares whether a tool saves time with patients, not whether it improves enterprise reporting. Ease of use must be designed and tested with real users in real contexts. Usability testing, task analysis and iterative design are not optional refinements. They directly shape the beliefs that determine whether adoption begins at all.
bullets: Show usefulness in terms of the user's goals, not the organization's.
Test ease of use with real users performing real tasks.
Remove steps and decisions that add effort without adding value.
Ensure early experiences reinforce, rather than contradict, promised benefits.

sections.heading: Social influence and diffusion
paragraphs: Everett Rogers' diffusion of innovations describes how new ideas and technologies spread through social systems over time. Rogers observed that people adopt at different points, from early adopters who are drawn to novelty to later adopters who wait for evidence and social proof. He also identified characteristics that make an innovation spread more readily: relative advantage over existing options, compatibility with current values and practices, low complexity, the ability to try it on a limited basis, and visible results.

These ideas are especially relevant inside organizations. People watch what respected colleagues do, and informal opinion leaders often influence adoption more than formal announcements. Peer champions, visible early successes and opportunities to try a technology with low risk all speed diffusion. Conversely, when influential people resist or quietly avoid a new system, others follow. Understanding the social network around adoption is as important as understanding the technology itself. Mapping who people turn to for advice often reveals the most effective path for spreading new practices.

sections.heading: Habit, identity and resistance
paragraphs: Even when a new technology is useful and easy, existing habits compete with it. Established routines are efficient and require little thought, so switching to a new tool imposes a cost in attention and effort, at least at first. People may also feel that their expertise, built around old systems, is devalued. In professional settings, technology can seem to threaten autonomy, status or the quality of work people take pride in. These concerns are often expressed as resistance, but they are usually reasonable responses to real costs.

Effective adoption strategies take these concerns seriously. They involve users early in design, make the transition gradual where possible, protect the value of existing expertise and respect autonomy in how tools are used. The Fogg Behavior Model helps here: a new behavior needs adequate motivation, sufficient ability and a timely prompt, and it must eventually become a habit of its own. Leaders who listen to resistance often discover design flaws worth fixing.
bullets: Old routines are efficient and resist replacement.
New tools can feel like a threat to expertise or autonomy.
Resistance often signals real design or workflow problems.
Gradual transitions and early involvement reduce friction.

sections.heading: Measuring adoption with predictive signals
paragraphs: Most organizations measure adoption with lagging indicators such as licenses activated, logins or overall usage at the end of a quarter. These numbers say little about whether people are using the technology meaningfully or whether usage will last. More predictive measures focus on early behaviors that precede sustained use, such as completing a first real task, returning within the first weeks or using a core feature repeatedly. These behaviors indicate whether the technology is becoming part of real work rather than a box people check.

Identifying these signals requires behavioral data analysis. Compare the early usage patterns of people who become sustained users with those who drop away, and look for the moments where their paths diverge. Those moments are conversion points for adoption, and the behaviors at those points become predictive KPIs. Segmenting users by behavior, rather than by role or department alone, reveals who needs what kind of support and when. Some users need simpler first steps, others need evidence of value, and others need a peer to show them how.

sections.heading: How Datalidy applies the psychology of technology adoption
paragraphs: Datalidy brings human-computer interaction, persuasive technology and behavioral science together in its approach to technology adoption. In the Observe phase of its Observe, Signal, Design, Test, Scale method, the firm studies how people actually work through contextual inquiry and usability testing. In Signal, behavioral data analysis identifies the early usage behaviors that predict lasting adoption. In Design, onboarding, workflows, messaging and peer support are shaped to address usefulness, ease of use, social influence and habit.

The Test phase validates these interventions through pilots and A/B tests, and the Scale phase supports rollout with dashboards, change management and leadership coaching. The firm applies this approach to customer-facing products, clinical and digital health tools, internal enterprise systems and responsible AI adoption. In each case, the aim is lasting, meaningful use that helps people do their work better, not just higher login counts. Because adoption depends on trust as much as features, the firm pays close attention to transparency and to the concerns users raise along the way.

faqs.q: What is the Technology Acceptance Model?
faqs.a: The Technology Acceptance Model, developed by Fred Davis, proposes that people's intention to use a technology depends mainly on two perceptions: how useful they believe it will be and how easy they believe it will be to use. The model has been extended many times to include factors such as social influence and facilitating conditions, but those two core beliefs remain a practical starting point for adoption strategy.

faqs.q: Why do employees resist new systems even when they are better?
faqs.a: Because better in principle can still be costly in practice. Learning a new system takes time and attention, disrupts efficient routines and may make hard-won expertise less relevant. People may also doubt that promised benefits will materialize for them. Understanding these costs through direct observation and conversation, then designing to reduce them, is usually more effective than additional mandates or communication.

faqs.q: How soon can we tell whether adoption is working?
faqs.a: Often much sooner than lagging usage reports suggest. Early behaviors, such as completing a first meaningful task or returning within a short period, frequently predict whether someone will become a sustained user. Identifying and tracking these behaviors gives leaders an early read on adoption and time to adjust onboarding, support or design before problems become entrenched.

insights.title: Habit Formation for Products and Organizations
insights.meta_title: Habit Formation for Products and Organizations
insights.meta_description: The science of habit formation applied to products and organizations: cues, routines, rewards and context, and how to design behaviors that persist ethically.
insights.summary: How habits form, why they matter for products and organizations, and how to design cues, routines and contexts that help valuable behaviors persist over time.
insights.dek: Much of what people do each day happens on autopilot. Understanding habit formation helps organizations design products, services and workplaces where valuable behaviors persist without constant effort or reminders.
key_takeaways: Habits are behaviors triggered automatically by context cues, built through repetition in stable settings rather than through motivation alone.
Products become habitual when a valuable action is easy, repeated in a consistent context and followed by a satisfying result.
Organizational habits, such as how meetings run or decisions are reviewed, shape culture and performance as much as formal strategy.
Ethical habit design helps people sustain behaviors they value and avoids engineering compulsive use against their interests.

sections.heading: What a habit is
paragraphs: A habit is a behavior that has become largely automatic, triggered by a cue in the environment rather than by a conscious decision. Psychological research on habit formation describes a process in which a behavior repeated in a stable context gradually becomes linked to that context. Over time, the context alone is enough to prompt the behavior, with little deliberation required. Brushing teeth after waking, checking a phone when it buzzes or reaching for a familiar tool at the start of a task are all examples.

Habits matter because they are efficient and durable. They free attention for other things, and they persist even when motivation fluctuates. This is precisely why they are so important for products, health and organizations. Behaviors that depend on daily decisions are vulnerable to distraction, fatigue and competing priorities. Behaviors that have become habits continue with much less effort. Understanding habit formation helps explain why some behaviors stick and others fade after an initial burst of enthusiasm.

sections.heading: The building blocks of habit formation
paragraphs: Most accounts of habit formation describe three elements. A cue signals that it is time to act. A routine is the behavior itself. A reward, or more generally a satisfying outcome, reinforces the link between cue and routine. With repetition in a consistent context, the link strengthens until the cue triggers the routine automatically. Researchers emphasize that repetition and context stability are central, and that the time required to form a habit varies widely between people and behaviors.

B.J. Fogg's work offers a complementary perspective. His Behavior Model holds that behavior happens when motivation, ability and a prompt converge, and his approach to tiny habits suggests anchoring a very small new behavior to an existing routine and reinforcing it with a positive emotion. Making the behavior small increases ability, anchoring it provides a reliable prompt, and positive emotion helps it stick. Starting small also reduces the dependence on motivation, which is the least reliable element.
bullets: Cue: a consistent context or event that prompts the behavior.
Routine: a behavior simple enough to repeat reliably.
Reward: a satisfying outcome that reinforces the link.
Repetition: frequent practice in a stable context.
Anchoring: attaching the new behavior to an established routine.

sections.heading: Habit formation in products and services
paragraphs: For products and services, habit formation often determines long-term retention. A product people use habitually becomes part of their routine and is less likely to be replaced. Designing for habit means identifying the core action that delivers value, making it as easy as possible, connecting it to a natural cue in the user's day and ensuring it reliably produces a satisfying result. Onboarding plays a critical role, because early repetitions establish whether a behavior has a chance to become automatic.

Behavioral data reveals whether habits are forming. Look at whether usage becomes more regular and context-consistent over time, and whether people return without external prompts such as reminders or promotions. Users who develop stable patterns of use early often behave very differently from those whose usage is sporadic. Identifying the behaviors that distinguish these groups provides predictive KPIs for retention and points to the moments where design can support habit formation.

sections.heading: Habits inside organizations
paragraphs: Organizations have habits too. How meetings begin, how decisions are recorded, how feedback is given, how new information is shared and how problems are escalated are often governed by routine rather than by policy. These organizational habits shape culture more powerfully than values statements, because they determine what people actually do every day. When an organization tries to change its strategy without changing its habits, the old routines frequently reassert themselves.

Changing organizational habits follows similar principles to individual habits. Identify the cue, the routine and the reward currently in place, then design a new routine that responds to the same cue and delivers a satisfying result. Make the new behavior small and easy at first, anchor it to existing rhythms such as weekly meetings, and reinforce it visibly. Leaders play a disproportionate role, because their own habits act as cues and models for everyone else.
bullets: Meeting routines that shape how decisions are made.
Feedback habits that determine what problems surface early.
Escalation patterns that govern how quickly issues are addressed.
Leadership behaviors that model what is normal for teams.

sections.heading: Ethical habit design
paragraphs: Habit formation can be used well or badly. Designing products to be habit-forming can help people maintain behaviors they value, such as exercising, taking medication, saving or learning. It can also be used to encourage compulsive use that serves a company's engagement metrics at the user's expense. Infinite feeds, unpredictable rewards designed to hold attention and notifications engineered to pull people back are familiar examples of habit design that many users later regret.

A practical ethical test is whether the habit serves the person's own goals and whether they would endorse it on reflection. Good habit design makes valuable behaviors easier and more automatic, respects people's time and attention, and makes it easy to stop. Measuring success by outcomes that matter to the user, such as health, learning or financial wellbeing, rather than by time spent alone helps keep habit design aligned with the person's interests.

sections.heading: How Datalidy applies habit formation
paragraphs: Datalidy applies habit formation science across consumer products, digital health, member programs and organizational change. Through its Behavioral Signals Design methodology, the firm identifies the early behaviors that predict whether a habit is forming and turns them into predictive KPIs. In the Observe phase, research reveals the natural cues and contexts in people's routines. In the Design phase, behavioral design and onboarding design make the core behavior small, easy, well-anchored and satisfying.

Interventions are validated through A/B tests and pilots in the Test phase, then embedded in the Scale phase through dashboards, process design and coaching. Inside organizations, Datalidy works with leaders and teams to redesign the routines that shape culture and decision-making. Throughout, the firm follows a clear principle: habit design should help people do what they already want to do, more easily and consistently, never trap them in behaviors they would not choose.

faqs.q: How long does it take to form a habit?
faqs.a: There is no single answer. Research indicates that the time required varies widely depending on the person, the complexity of the behavior and the consistency of the context. Simple behaviors repeated daily in the same setting tend to become automatic faster than complex or irregular ones. Popular claims about a fixed number of days oversimplify the evidence and should not guide product or program design.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a habit and a routine?
faqs.a: A routine is a sequence of behavior that someone performs regularly, which may still require deliberate effort and decision. A habit is a behavior triggered automatically by a cue, with little conscious thought. Routines can become habits through repetition in a stable context, and many effective programs aim to turn a deliberate routine into an automatic one over time.

faqs.q: Can organizations really change their habits?
faqs.a: Yes, though it requires deliberate design rather than announcements. Organizational habits are maintained by cues, routines and rewards embedded in meetings, systems and leadership behavior. Changing them involves redesigning those elements, starting small, anchoring new routines to existing rhythms and reinforcing them visibly. Leaders who model the new behavior consistently make it far more likely to spread and persist.

insights.title: Behavioral Design for Medication Adherence
insights.meta_description: How behavioral design improves medication adherence: why patients miss doses, what behavioral science suggests, and how to design and test better support.
insights.summary: Why medication adherence is a behavioral challenge, and how behavioral design, patient research and careful testing can help people take medicines as they intend.
insights.dek: Medicines only work when they are taken. Medication adherence depends on a chain of everyday behaviors, and behavioral design offers practical, respectful ways to make each link in that chain stronger.
key_takeaways: Medication adherence is a sequence of behaviors, from filling a first prescription to taking doses consistently over time.
Nonadherence has many causes, including forgetfulness, cost, side effects, complex regimens, beliefs about medicine and gaps in support.
Effective interventions match the specific barrier, which means understanding which patients struggle at which moments and why.
Respectful, patient-centered design treats adherence as a shared goal and helps people act on their own health intentions.

sections.heading: Why medication adherence is a behavioral challenge
paragraphs: Medication adherence refers to the extent to which people take medicines as agreed with their clinicians: the right dose, at the right time, for the intended duration. Poor adherence is widely recognized in healthcare as a major obstacle to effective treatment, particularly for chronic conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and many mental health conditions. When patients do not take medicines as intended, treatments that work in clinical trials may work far less well in everyday life.

Adherence is not a single decision. It is a chain of behaviors that includes accepting a diagnosis, agreeing to a treatment plan, filling the first prescription, starting the medicine, taking it at the right times, refilling before running out and continuing when symptoms improve or side effects appear. Each link in the chain can break for different reasons. That is why adherence is fundamentally a behavioral design problem, not only a clinical or educational one.

sections.heading: Why people miss doses
paragraphs: Health researchers often distinguish between unintentional and intentional nonadherence. Unintentional nonadherence happens when people mean to take their medicine but forget, run out, become confused by a complex regimen or face practical barriers such as cost, transport or pharmacy access. Intentional nonadherence happens when people decide not to take a medicine as prescribed, often because of side effects, doubts about whether it is necessary, worries about long-term use or a sense that they feel fine without it.

These categories call for different responses. Reminders and simplified regimens may help someone who forgets, but they will not help someone who has concerns about side effects or who does not believe the medicine is needed. Health behavior models, including the health belief model and frameworks grounded in self-determination theory, highlight the role of perceived benefits, perceived barriers, confidence and autonomy. Effective support starts by understanding which barriers apply to which patients.
bullets: Forgetting, especially with multiple daily doses.
Cost and insurance barriers at the pharmacy.
Side effects that reduce quality of life.
Complex regimens involving several medicines at different times.
Beliefs that the medicine is unnecessary or harmful.
Limited support from family, clinicians or care teams.

sections.heading: Applying behavioral design principles
paragraphs: The Fogg Behavior Model offers a useful lens: taking a medicine requires motivation, ability and a prompt at the same moment. Ability can be increased by simplifying regimens, synchronizing refills, using blister packs or pill organizers, enabling automatic refills and reducing out-of-pocket cost where possible. Prompts can be improved by anchoring doses to existing routines, such as a morning coffee or evening teeth brushing, and by well-timed reminders that arrive when patients are able to act.

Motivation is best supported through respectful communication rather than pressure. Clear explanations of how a medicine works, what to expect and how to manage side effects help patients make informed choices. Shared decision-making, in which clinicians and patients agree on a plan together, supports autonomy, which self-determination theory identifies as important for sustained behavior change. Habit formation principles also apply: once taking a medicine becomes an automatic part of a daily routine, it depends far less on memory or motivation.

sections.heading: Using data to target the right moments
paragraphs: Adherence data is often fragmented across pharmacy claims, electronic health records, patient apps, call center notes and program enrollment systems. Connecting these sources around the patient journey reveals where adherence typically breaks down. For many conditions, the critical moments are early: whether a first prescription is filled, whether the first refill happens on time, or whether a patient returns after an initial side effect. These are conversion points for adherence.

Behavioral segmentation adds precision. Patients who miss refills by a few days behave differently from those who stop entirely, and those who stop after a side effect differ from those who stop when they feel better. Grouping patients by behavior allows programs to match interventions to needs, such as practical support for some and a conversation with a pharmacist or clinician for others. Predictive KPIs built around these early behaviors give care teams time to help before adherence fails completely.
bullets: Track first fill and first refill timing as early signals.
Segment patients by adherence pattern, not only by diagnosis.
Match interventions to the barrier each segment faces.
Give care teams early alerts while there is still time to help.

sections.heading: Testing and ethical safeguards
paragraphs: Adherence interventions should be tested rather than assumed to work. A reminder message, a refill synchronization program or a pharmacist outreach call may help one population and have little effect on another. Structured pilots and, where appropriate, randomized comparisons between reasonable alternatives show what actually improves behavior. Outcome measures should focus on adherence behaviors and, where possible, on health outcomes, not merely on message opens or program enrollment. Results should also be examined by patient segment, since an average effect can conceal very different responses.

Ethical safeguards are essential in health settings. Every option tested should be acceptable care. Patient data must be protected and used in line with privacy rules and patient expectations. Communication should respect autonomy, recognizing that patients may have legitimate reasons for their choices and that the goal is informed decision-making, not compliance at any cost. Programs should also be checked for equity, ensuring they do not widen gaps between groups with different resources or access.

sections.heading: How Datalidy applies behavioral design to medication adherence
paragraphs: Datalidy's work on medication adherence draws on its roots in clinical and health psychology, behavioral medicine and persuasive technology. In the Observe phase of its Observe, Signal, Design, Test, Scale method, the firm conducts patient and clinician research to understand barriers in context. In the Signal phase, its Behavioral Signals Design methodology connects fragmented health data to identify adherence conversion points, behavioral types and predictive KPIs that give care teams earlier signals.

In the Design phase, the firm develops patient engagement strategies, digital health features, health communication and care team workflows that address specific barriers. The Test phase validates them through pilots and appropriate experiments, and the Scale phase supports implementation through dashboards and team coaching. Datalidy works with health systems, digital health companies and health-related organizations, always guided by the principle that behavioral science should help patients do what they already want to do for their own health.

faqs.q: Are reminders enough to improve medication adherence?
faqs.a: Reminders help some patients, particularly those who intend to take their medicine but forget. They are much less effective for patients facing cost barriers, side effects or doubts about whether a medicine is necessary. The most effective programs identify which barriers apply to which patients and combine approaches, such as simplified regimens, refill synchronization, clear communication and clinician conversations, rather than relying on reminders alone.

faqs.q: How can digital health products support adherence?
faqs.a: Digital health products can provide well-timed prompts, simplify tracking, connect patients with care teams and deliver education at the right moment. Their effectiveness depends on design: they must be easy to use, relevant to the patient's routine and respectful of autonomy. Engagement with the product itself also needs to be sustained, which requires the same behavioral design attention as adherence.

faqs.q: Is it ethical to use behavioral science to influence medication taking?
faqs.a: It can be, when it supports patients' own health goals and respects their autonomy. Ethical adherence programs help people act on treatment decisions they have made with their clinicians, provide honest information and make it easier to follow through. They do not pressure, shame or deceive. Transparency, privacy protection and respect for informed choice are essential safeguards in any health behavior program.

insights.title: The Ethics of Persuasive Technology
insights.meta_title: The Ethics of Persuasive Technology: A Practical Guide
insights.meta_description: The ethics of persuasive technology: where influence becomes manipulation, how to spot dark patterns, and principles for designing behavior change responsibly.
insights.summary: Where persuasion ends and manipulation begins in digital products and services, and practical principles for designing behavior change that respects people's interests and autonomy.
insights.dek: Every interface influences behavior. The question is not whether technology persuades, but whether it does so transparently and in people's interest. Clear ethical principles help organizations design persuasive technology they can stand behind.
key_takeaways: Persuasive technology is any interactive system designed to change attitudes or behaviors, a field B.J. Fogg helped define.
Persuasion becomes manipulation when it relies on deception, exploits vulnerabilities or works against the interests of the person influenced.
Dark patterns and sludge erode trust and invite regulatory scrutiny, even when they lift short-term metrics.
Ethical design starts with aligned goals, transparency, respect for autonomy and measures that reflect user wellbeing, not only engagement.

sections.heading: What persuasive technology is
paragraphs: Persuasive technology refers to interactive computing systems designed to change people's attitudes or behaviors. B.J. Fogg helped establish the field at Stanford, describing how computers can act as tools that make behaviors easier, as media that provide experiences, and as social actors that people respond to as they would to other people. Today persuasive technology is everywhere: fitness apps that encourage activity, financial tools that prompt saving, onboarding flows that guide new users and notifications that bring people back.

Fogg emphasized from the beginning that persuasive technology raises distinct ethical questions. Interactive systems can be persistent, personalized and available at any moment, and they can operate at a scale no human persuader could match. They can also obscure who is doing the persuading and why. These features make persuasive technology powerful for good, such as supporting health or learning, and equally powerful for harm when it is used to serve narrow interests at people's expense.

sections.heading: Persuasion versus manipulation
paragraphs: The central ethical question is where legitimate persuasion ends and manipulation begins. Persuasion appeals to reasons, emotions or social cues in ways that a person could recognize and endorse. Manipulation bypasses or exploits a person's decision-making in ways they would reject if they understood what was happening. The distinction is not always sharp, but several markers help: whether the intent is disclosed, whether the methods involve deception, whether the influence exploits a particular vulnerability and whether the outcome serves the person influenced.

Thaler and Sunstein drew a similar line for nudges, arguing that legitimate nudges preserve freedom of choice and aim to help people by their own standards. Influence that works only because people do not notice it, or that relies on confusion, false urgency or hidden costs, fails that test. A practical check is publicity: would the organization be comfortable explaining exactly how and why the technology influences behavior to the people affected, and to a regulator?
bullets: Intent: is the goal of influence disclosed or concealed?
Methods: does it rely on accurate information or deception?
Vulnerability: does it exploit fatigue, distress or limited understanding?
Outcome: does it serve the person, or only the organization?

sections.heading: Dark patterns and sludge
paragraphs: Dark patterns are interface designs that steer people toward choices they might not make with full understanding. Common examples include subscriptions that are easy to start and hard to cancel, pre-checked boxes that add unwanted services, confusing wording that makes declining feel like a mistake, fake scarcity or countdown timers, and hidden fees revealed only at the last step. Sludge is a related term for unnecessary friction that makes beneficial actions harder, such as complicated refund processes or burdensome paperwork.

These practices may improve short-term metrics, but they carry real costs. They damage trust, generate complaints, increase churn once customers realize what happened, and attract regulatory attention, as consumer protection authorities in several jurisdictions have increasingly focused on deceptive design. Most importantly, they harm people. In health, finance and education, manipulative design can have serious consequences for wellbeing. Organizations that rely on these patterns are building on a fragile foundation.
bullets: Hard-to-cancel subscriptions and hidden renewal terms.
Pre-selected add-ons that people did not request.
False urgency, scarcity claims or countdown timers.
Confusing language that makes declining feel risky.
Unnecessary friction that blocks beneficial actions.

sections.heading: Principles for ethical persuasive design
paragraphs: Ethical persuasive technology starts with aligned goals. The behavior being encouraged should be one the person already values or would endorse on reflection, such as maintaining their health, saving money, learning a skill or completing a task they started. Transparency follows: people should be able to understand what the system is trying to do and why. Autonomy matters too. People should be able to decline, opt out, change settings and leave without penalty or excessive effort.

Attention to vulnerability is also essential. Persuasive techniques that are acceptable for a typical adult may be inappropriate for children, people in distress, people with limited literacy or people facing financial hardship. Measurement shapes ethics as well. When teams are rewarded only for engagement, time on site or conversion, they will find ways to increase those numbers, sometimes at users' expense. Including measures of user benefit and satisfaction alongside business metrics keeps design incentives aligned with people's interests.

sections.heading: Making ethics operational
paragraphs: Ethical principles only matter if they shape decisions. Organizations can make them operational in several ways. Design reviews can include explicit questions about intent, methods, vulnerability and outcome. Experiments can be reviewed for ethical acceptability before launch, ensuring every version tested is one the organization would be comfortable deploying. Teams can maintain a list of prohibited patterns and examine new features against it. Assigning clear ownership for these reviews, rather than leaving ethics to individual conscience, makes it far more likely that concerns are raised before launch rather than after complaints arrive.

Research is a valuable safeguard. Usability testing and interviews reveal whether people understand what a system is doing and whether they feel respected or tricked. Monitoring complaints, cancellations and support requests can surface problems that metrics miss. Leaders play a decisive role by making clear that short-term gains achieved through manipulation are not acceptable, and by rewarding teams for outcomes that benefit both the organization and the people it serves.
bullets: Add ethical questions to design and experiment reviews.
Maintain a list of prohibited dark patterns.
Test comprehension and perceived fairness with real users.
Balance engagement metrics with measures of user benefit.

sections.heading: How Datalidy approaches the ethics of persuasive technology
paragraphs: Persuasive technology is one of the disciplines at the root of Datalidy's practice, alongside human-computer interaction, clinical and health psychology and behavioral medicine. The firm's position is clear: behavioral science should help people do what they already want to do, never manipulate them. That principle shapes every phase of its Observe, Signal, Design, Test, Scale method, from the outcomes chosen for predictive KPIs to the interventions designed and the experiments approved.

In practice, Datalidy helps organizations design persuasive technology that is effective and trustworthy, review existing products for manipulative patterns and build governance for responsible AI adoption and behavioral design. Its work in health, education, financial services and the social sector reflects a commitment to public health, patient wellbeing and the ethical use of persuasion. Ethics is not treated as a constraint on performance, but as a condition for durable results.

faqs.q: Is all persuasive technology manipulative?
faqs.a: No. Persuasive technology includes many systems that help people achieve their own goals, such as apps that support exercise, saving or medication routines. What makes persuasion ethical is alignment with the person's interests, transparency about intent, accurate information and respect for autonomy. Manipulation occurs when influence relies on deception, exploits vulnerabilities or serves the organization at the person's expense.

faqs.q: What are dark patterns?
faqs.a: Dark patterns are design choices that steer people toward decisions they might not make with full understanding, often benefiting the organization at the user's expense. Examples include hidden fees, pre-checked add-ons, difficult cancellation processes, false urgency and confusing wording. They can raise short-term metrics but tend to damage trust, increase complaints and attract regulatory scrutiny.

faqs.q: How can teams balance business goals with ethical design?
faqs.a: Start by choosing goals that serve both the organization and its users, then measure both. Include indicators of user benefit, comprehension and satisfaction alongside conversion or engagement. Review designs and experiments against clear ethical principles before launch. Over time, trustworthy design tends to support retention, reputation and lifetime value, which makes ethics and performance more aligned than they first appear.
